title: Goods that cannot travel on Saturday
body: Yehuda is a Jewish merchant, and Saturday is his day of rest. Some of his goods must go by road on that day to reach the river boat. He asks if one of your carters can take them.

choices.label: Send your carter with the goods
choices.hint: It costs a day of your carter and 5 dinars. Yehuda will owe you a favour.

choices.label: Say you are too busy
choices.hint: Your carter earns 4 dinars on your own goods, and the street sees a house with steady work. Yehuda will ask someone else.

note: North African Jewish traders in the Geniza letters had long given goods for the road to Muslim business friends. That way no Jewish carrier had to travel on the Sabbath.

sources.at: p. 281, as quoted by Edwards and Ogilvie (2008), p. 17

title: A Christian merchant writes
body: Nicola is a Christian merchant in Alexandria. He has heard good things of your house and wants to trade with you. He asks you to send him a few bolts of linen to start.

choices.label: Send him the linen
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now and pays back 5 in three seasons. He may become a steady friend.

choices.label: Ask for a letter from someone you know
choices.hint: It costs nothing. He starts with a small order.

note: Traders of different faiths had long done business together. Around 1030 one Jewish firm dealt with Christians in Alexandria, as two historians report it from Moshe Gil.

sources.at: p. 17; dealings with Christian merchants in Alexandria, citing Gil (2004), p. 687

title: A neighbour goes to Mecca
body: Hajar has saved for years to make the pilgrimage, the holy journey to Mecca. She asks to travel with your carters as far as Qus. She cannot pay much.

choices.label: Take her at no charge
choices.hint: It costs a little. Your street will hear of it.

choices.label: Ask a small fee for her seat
choices.hint: You are paid. Your neighbours may talk.

note: In May 1326 Ibn Battuta left Cairo for Upper Egypt, on his way to Mecca by the Red Sea road through Aydhab. A writer of the 1180s says Saladin had ended the tax on pilgrims at Aydhab.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 58 to 59; he left Cairo by the Upper Egypt road for the Hijaz, May 1326
p. 34; Saladin repealed the tax on pilgrims at Aydhab, from Ibn Jubayr
